CONFIDENCE: 95

Yes. Absolute advantage in both goods does not preclude mutual gains. What matters is comparative advantage: each country should specialize in the good with the lower opportunity cost (the good it produces relatively more efficiently) and trade for the other. As long as the countries’ relative productivities differ, specialization and exchange can raise consumption of both goods in both countries above autarky levels.

CONFIDENCE: 95

Research finds that strict rent control mainly reduces the supply and quality of rental housing, misallocates units, and raises uncontrolled rents, while shielding only incumbent tenants.

Landlords respond to binding caps by converting rentals to owner-occupied or other uses, deferring maintenance, and cutting new construction, which shrinks the rental stock (often by double-digit percentages in studied cities). Tenants who already hold controlled units stay longer than they otherwise would, producing shortages and mismatches between household size and unit size. Newcomers and movers face tighter availability and higher rents in the uncontrolled segment. These patterns appear consistently in empirical studies of places such as San Francisco, Cambridge, and other tightly regulated markets.

CONFIDENCE: 88

The statutory (legal) incidence of the corporate income tax falls on corporations, but economic incidence—who actually bears the burden through lower returns, wages, or higher prices—is different and is determined by market responses.

In standard models (starting from Harberger), a tax on corporate capital reduces the after-tax return to capital. Capital then reallocates toward the non-corporate sector until after-tax returns are equalized, so the burden is shared by owners of capital economy-wide rather than only by corporate shareholders. In an open economy with mobile capital, part of the burden is shifted onto the immobile factor (labor) via lower wages; some may also be passed forward to consumers via higher prices, depending on product-market competition and demand elasticities. The precise shares are not settled: official scoring assumptions (e.g., CBO) often assign roughly three-quarters to capital owners and one-quarter to labor, while empirical estimates range more widely. Short-run incidence falls more heavily on existing shareholders; long-run incidence is more diffuse.

Thus the economic burden is shared among capital owners, workers, and (to a lesser extent) consumers, not borne solely by the corporations that remit the tax.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. The shift away from lead in U.S. household paint was already well underway decades before the 1978 federal ban.

Lead pigments and driers had been common in interior and exterior paints for durability and opacity, but safer white pigments (especially titanium dioxide) and other substitutes became commercially available in the early–mid 20th century. Health concerns about childhood lead poisoning also prompted earlier action: some cities restricted lead paint in the 1950s, and in 1955 the paint industry adopted a voluntary standard limiting lead in interior paints to 1 percent. Federal law followed that trend rather than initiating it—the 1971 Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Prevention Act and related rules tightened limits further, and by the mid-1970s most residential paints already contained little or no lead. The 1978 CPSC rule (banning residential paint above 0.06 percent lead) largely locked in a transition that manufacturers, local rules, and market substitution had already begun.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Vaccination often generates positive externalities that private decisions do not fully internalize, so subsidies or requirements can raise social welfare even after medical benefits to the recipient are set aside.

When a person is vaccinated, transmission risk to others falls. That protects people who cannot be vaccinated, reduces outbreaks, and can push coverage toward herd-immunity thresholds that benefit the whole population. The social return therefore exceeds the private return whenever infection is contagious. Standard externality theory then implies under-vaccination in an unsubsidized market: people weigh their own risk reduction, side-effect risk, time cost, and out-of-pocket price, but not the full value of infections they would otherwise cause. A subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit, or a requirement that achieves a similar coverage level, can close that gap.

Related economic channels reinforce the case. Unvaccinated illness imposes costs on insurers, public payers, employers (absenteeism, disrupted production), and hospitals (capacity congestion). Those are pecuniary or fiscal externalities, not only epidemiological ones. Dynamic effects matter too: widespread vaccination can slow variant emergence and preserve the value of existing vaccines. Cost-benefit studies of routine childhood vaccines, influenza, and COVID-19 shots repeatedly find social benefits well above private and program costs once transmission and healthcare spillovers are counted; many of those programs are already subsidized or mandated for that reason.

The case is not uniform. It is weak for non-contagious diseases (tetanus is mostly a private good). It weakens if a vaccine poorly blocks transmission, if side effects are large, or if mandates are costly to enforce and politically brittle. In those settings a targeted subsidy, or no intervention, can dominate a blanket requirement. Where transmission externalities are large and vaccines are safe and effective, however, the economic argument for subsidizing or requiring vaccination is standard and well supported.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Cities that introduced congestion pricing have generally found substantial drops in traffic volumes and delays inside the charged zones, faster and more reliable trips, lower vehicle emissions, and shifts toward public transit, with net social benefits and public acceptance that often rises after people experience the results.

London’s central charge (from 2003), Stockholm’s cordon (trial 2006, permanent from 2007), and Singapore’s area licensing/electronic road pricing (from the 1970s/1998) are the main long-running cases. Independent evaluations and official monitoring consistently report entry or peak traffic reductions on the order of about 10–30 percent, larger cuts in congestion delay because of the nonlinear relationship between volume and speed, better bus reliability, and measurable air-quality gains. Revenue has typically been earmarked for transit and other transport improvements. Feared large losses to retail and business activity have mostly not materialized; accessibility gains often offset the charge for many trips. Political support has frequently increased once the schemes were in place and the travel-time benefits were visible.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Economic research finds small or negligible effects overall. Landmark studies (e.g., Card on the Mariel Boatlift) and syntheses such as the 2017 National Academies of Sciences report generally estimate little to no wage reduction for native-born workers as a group. Where negative effects appear, they are concentrated among the least-skilled natives (especially high-school dropouts) and prior immigrants, and are typically only a few percentage points; other work (including studies emphasizing imperfect substitutability) finds effects near zero. Results remain somewhat sensitive to assumptions about skill groups and time horizons, but large adverse wage impacts are not the central finding of the literature.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Yes. Phasing out leaded gasoline and restricting lead paint produced large, well-documented net benefits that substantially exceeded the transition costs.

Lead is a cumulative neurotoxin with no known safe exposure level. Population blood-lead levels fell sharply after the U.S. gasoline phase-down (1970s–1996) and the 1978 residential paint ban—from roughly 15 µg/dL in children in the late 1970s to well under 1 µg/dL in recent national surveys. That decline tracks reduced emissions and new paint sources, not merely better measurement.

The health gains are large and causal in direction: higher childhood lead exposure lowers IQ, impairs attention and impulse control, and raises risks of hypertension, kidney disease, and cardiovascular mortality later in life. Cohort and quasi-experimental studies that exploit the timing of gasoline lead reductions find IQ and behavioral improvements consistent with the toxicology. Economic valuations of those effects—mainly avoided cognitive losses, healthcare costs, and premature mortality—run into the hundreds of billions to trillions of dollars in present-value terms for the United States alone, far above the costs of reformulated gasoline, catalytic-converter compatibility, and alternative pigments.

Remaining lead hazards (old paint, soil, water pipes) are legacy problems created by earlier use, not evidence that the phase-out itself was harmful. Claims that the regulations were net costly, or that observed gains are wholly explained by unrelated trends, do not match the exposure data or the dose–response evidence.

CONFIDENCE: 92

No. Heritability estimates the share of *observed differences among people* (in a given population and range of environments) that is associated with genetic differences. It says nothing about how much the average level of the trait can shift if the environment changes, nor about whether an intervention can alter the trait for individuals.

Classic counterexamples include height (highly heritable, yet population means rose sharply with nutrition and health) and PKU-related intellectual disability (genetically caused, yet largely prevented by diet). Heritability can also change when environments change, because it is a population statistic, not a fixed property of the trait.

CONFIDENCE: 95

Occupational licensing (state-mandated education, exams, fees, and permission to practice) has been studied extensively by labor economists, including work associated with Morris Kleiner and summaries from the FTC and the 2015 White House report on the topic. The main documented effects, especially for lower-risk occupations such as barbers, cosmetologists, florists, and many contractor trades, are:

- Higher earnings for those who obtain licenses (typically on the order of 10–15 percent), consistent with reduced competition.
- Lower employment and slower entry into the occupation, because training time, fees, and exam requirements screen out workers.
- Higher prices for consumers.
- Weaker geographic mobility, since requirements differ across states and are often not reciprocal.
- Little consistent evidence of better service quality, safety, or consumer outcomes for many of the cited occupations; quality effects are more plausible in high-stakes fields (e.g., medicine) than for barbering or floristry.
- Disproportionate barriers for lower-income workers, immigrants, and people with criminal records, who are less able to absorb the upfront costs.

These patterns are rent-seeking and supply-restriction effects more than demonstrated public-safety gains in the examples given.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Moderate city-level minimum-wage hikes of 10–15% generally produce little or no detectable drop in overall employment. High-quality studies that exploit border discontinuities, bunching at the new wage floor, or synthetic controls (including multi-state panels and city-specific episodes) typically estimate employment elasticities near zero for the broader low-wage workforce; any losses that appear are concentrated among teenagers or the lowest-skilled workers and are usually small (on the order of 1–3% fewer jobs or hours for a 10% wage increase). Total earnings of low-wage workers therefore tend to rise. Larger or rapidly phased-in increases can generate clearer hours reductions, but that is outside the moderate range specified here.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Personality traits such as extraversion and neuroticism are moderately heritable. Large-scale twin, adoption, and family studies (including meta-analyses) consistently find that genetic differences account for roughly 40–60% of the variance in these traits; the remainder is mostly non-shared environment (plus measurement error), with shared family environment contributing little.

CONFIDENCE: 85

No. Signature literacy (the standard historical proxy) was already widespread in England before a national system of state elementary schools existed. Marriage-register data show roughly two-thirds of men and half of women could sign their names by the early 1840s, rising to about 80% of men and 73% of women by 1870—the year of Forster’s Education Act. Compulsory attendance came only in 1880 and was enforced gradually thereafter. The long rise in literacy was driven mainly by private, charitable, church, and Sunday schools plus parental demand in a commercial society; limited state grants from the 1830s supplemented rather than created that trend. State schooling later universalized and standardized provision, but it did not originate mass literacy.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Large differences in pay for work are not inherently unfair when they arise from voluntary exchange and differences in the value people create for others.

Markets pay according to marginal productivity and scarcity: a surgeon, engineer, or founder whose decisions affect thousands of outcomes, or whose output scales to millions of users, generates far more revenue than someone whose work does not. Small gaps in skill, judgment, or timing produce outsized gaps in results in many fields (the “superstar” effect). Employers and customers willingly pay the premium because the alternative—underpaying scarce talent—costs them more. Equalizing pay regardless of contribution would itself be unfair to those who produce more, and it would reduce the incentive to acquire rare skills.

Unfairness enters when the gap is produced by coercion, fraud, legal barriers that block entry, or discrimination unrelated to performance—not from the mere existence of a 50-to-1 ratio. Luck and background matter, but they do not convert every large, consensual earnings difference into an injustice.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Standard Oil’s refining market share had already been eroding for years before the 1911 decree (from roughly 90 percent in the 1890s to about 64 percent by the time of dissolution) as new fields and independent refiners expanded. Over the same period the price of kerosene fell sharply and continued to decline, reflecting both technological gains and that growing competition.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. Multinational export factories in poor countries generally pay *better* than realistic local alternatives (subsistence farming, informal work, or many domestic firms), which is why workers compete for the jobs. Boycotts that shut those factories therefore tend to make the workers worse off, not better.

Empirical patterns, not slogans, drive this. Foreign-owned and export plants typically pay wage premiums—often on the order of 10–40% or more after accounting for worker traits—relative to domestic employers in the same labor markets (documented across apparel, electronics, and similar sectors in places such as Indonesia, Vietnam, Mexico, and Bangladesh). Those wages are still low by rich-country standards and hours and safety can be poor in absolute terms, but they are high enough *locally* that people leave worse options to take them. When demand collapses (boycotts, sudden order cancellations, or forced closures), the usual result is job loss and a return to lower-paid or more dangerous work, not an immediate jump to “good” jobs that did not exist. Broader development—productivity growth, education, and gradually tighter standards that do not price workers out—is what has historically raised pay, not consumer boycotts of the factories themselves.

CONFIDENCE: 82

No. Within-group heritability does not imply that a mean difference between groups is genetic.

Heritability is the fraction of *variance among individuals inside a population* that is associated with genetic differences, under the environments those individuals actually experience. A high value (as for IQ) means that, within each group, people who differ genetically tend to differ in IQ. It says nothing about why the *group averages* differ.

Between-group gaps can be produced entirely by environmental factors that differ systematically between the groups (nutrition, education, disease burden, cultural practices, discrimination, and so on), even when every within-group difference is largely genetic. The same logic applies to any trait: height is highly heritable within populations, yet large average height differences between cohorts or countries have been produced by environmental change. The classic illustration is genetically identical seed stocks grown in rich versus poor soil: within each plot, height differences are genetic; the difference between plot means is environmental.

Quantitatively, the genetic contribution to a group mean difference is not fixed by within-group heritability. It can range from zero to 100 percent depending on how large the environmental difference between groups is and how strongly those environments affect the trait. Establishing a partial genetic cause for a group difference therefore requires direct evidence about the groups (for example, adoption or migration designs that change environments while holding ancestry roughly constant, or genomic analyses of between-group allele-frequency differences that are shown to be causal). Within-group heritability alone does not supply that evidence.

CONFIDENCE: 95

The Federal Reserve was created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, primarily in response to repeated banking panics (notably 1873, 1893, and 1907) that exposed the absence of a lender of last resort and an elastic currency. Its original statutory aims were to furnish a flexible money supply, rediscount commercial paper, and improve bank supervision so as to reduce the frequency and severity of financial crises.

Its record against those aims is mixed. It has repeatedly supplied emergency liquidity (1987, 2008, 2020) and, together with deposit insurance and later regulatory reforms, has made classic bank runs rarer. Yet it failed to prevent or mitigate the monetary contraction of the early 1930s, accommodated the high inflation of the 1970s, and is widely argued to have contributed to credit booms that preceded the 2008 crisis and the 2021–22 inflation surge. Major banking stresses have continued to occur. Thus the institution has partially stabilized short-run liquidity conditions while falling short of delivering durable macroeconomic or financial stability.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Mass industrial child labor in the United States largely disappeared because rising adult wages and technological change made children’s earnings less necessary to households and less useful to employers, while the payoff to schooling rose. Census and labor-force data show the share of children aged 10–15 who were employed falling sharply from the early 1900s into the 1920s—well before the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. State child-labor and compulsory-schooling statutes, and later the federal ban, reinforced and locked in that decline (especially outside agriculture), but economic studies attribute only a modest share of the drop to the laws themselves. Agricultural child work lingered longer under exemptions and lower incomes.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Yes. Smallpox was eradicated by a deliberate, centrally coordinated public-health campaign—not by uncoordinated buying and selling of vaccines.

Jenner’s vaccine existed from the late 18th century and was commercially and philanthropically available for generations, yet endemic transmission continued in large parts of Africa, Asia, and South America into the 1960s. What ended the disease was the WHO Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme (from 1967), which combined mass and ring vaccination, active case-finding, containment, and cross-border surveillance, financed and staffed largely by governments and international public agencies. The last natural case was in 1977; eradication was certified in 1980.

Ordinary market activity alone was not a plausible substitute. Vaccination has strong positive externalities (herd effects and the global public good of eradication), so private willingness to pay falls short of the social value, especially once incidence is already low. Many endemic populations could not pay; information, logistics, and compulsory or quasi-compulsory containment crossed jurisdictions that no firm controlled. Historical evidence matches the theory: markets and charity supplied vaccine for nearly two centuries without achieving eradication; the coordinated public program did so in about a decade.

CONFIDENCE: 90

No. The Great Depression was already underway after the October 1929 stock-market crash and the subsequent collapse in output, prices, and credit; the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act was not signed until June 1930. Mainstream economic history attributes the Depression’s onset and depth primarily to monetary contraction, banking panics, and the constraints of the gold standard, not to the tariff.

Smoot-Hawley raised duties on many imports and prompted foreign retaliation, which reduced trade volumes. That effect was real but secondary: U.S. exports were only a small share of GDP, much of the trade decline reflected falling incomes and demand rather than the tariff schedule itself, and quantitative estimates put the Act’s contribution to the U.S. downturn well below the damage from monetary and financial collapse. It worsened an existing crisis; it did not cause it.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Yes. The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments’ Acid Rain Program (ARP)—a national SO2 cap-and-trade system for power plants, with a secondary NOx component—met its statutory emissions goals, did so at far lower cost than forecast, and produced measurable declines in acid deposition and related harms.

The law required roughly a 10-million-ton cut in utility SO2 from 1980 levels (about a 50% reduction), phased in from 1995 (Phase I) and 2000 (Phase II). Covered sources complied almost fully. SO2 emissions from the power sector fell well below the cap within a few years of each phase and have since declined by on the order of 90% from 1990 levels (later rules, cheaper scrubbers, and fuel switching amplified the trend, but the ARP itself delivered the early, binding cuts). Allowance trading was active; firms banked early reductions; and compliance costs came in at roughly $1–2 billion per year rather than the several-times-higher figures projected under command-and-control alternatives.

Ambient sulfate and wet sulfate deposition fell substantially across the eastern United States. Many lakes and streams showed reduced acidity and partial biological recovery; fine-particle and visibility co-benefits were large and, by EPA and independent estimates, health benefits exceeded program costs by a wide margin. Ecological recovery remains incomplete in some sensitive areas (soil base-cation depletion, ongoing nitrogen deposition, and climate factors slow full restoration), and NOx cuts under the original program were more modest than the SO2 cuts. Those limits do not overturn the core result: the cap was achieved, cheaply, with clear environmental improvement.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Migrant remittances to low- and middle-income countries are substantially larger than official development assistance (ODA). In recent years they have run on the order of $600–700 billion annually, roughly three times DAC ODA (around $200–220 billion). For many recipient countries they are also a larger and more reliable external inflow than aid.

Their economic profiles differ sharply. Remittances are private, person-to-person transfers that reach households directly; they are relatively stable and often counter-cyclical, and are used mainly for consumption, education, health, and small-scale investment. ODA is public, politically allocated, and usually channeled through governments or official projects (grants or concessional loans); it is more discretionary and volatile, and is aimed at public goods, infrastructure, or budget support rather than household income.

CONFIDENCE: 85

Municipal clean-water technologies (filtration and chlorination) accounted for roughly 43% of the total mortality decline in major U.S. cities between about 1900 and 1936 (and larger shares of the infant and child mortality declines). This is the central causal estimate from the difference-in-differences analysis in Cutler & Miller (2005).

CONFIDENCE: 62

Yes. The Montreal Protocol (1987, with later amendments) phased out the bulk of CFC and other ozone-depleting substance production and use. Measured atmospheric concentrations of the main CFCs have been falling for years, and the stratospheric ozone layer—including the Antarctic ozone hole—is on a documented recovery path, with mid-latitude recovery expected around mid-century and Antarctic recovery later in the century if compliance holds.

A treaty was required because CFCs are long-lived and well mixed: emissions anywhere thin the ozone layer everywhere. Unilateral national bans could not protect the global commons or stop free-riding, and coordinated phase-out (plus trade measures against non-parties and a fund for developing countries) was what made substitutes and compliance stick.

CONFIDENCE: 92

No. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which repealed the core affiliation barriers of the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act, was not a cause of the 2008 crisis.

The crisis was driven by a housing bubble fueled by subprime and Alt-A mortgage lending, the packaging of those loans into complex securities (MBS, CDOs), widespread use of credit default swaps, extreme leverage (especially among standalone investment banks and in the shadow-banking system), and failures of risk management and supervision. Those activities were already permissible—or were conducted by firms never covered by Glass-Steagall—well before 1999. The institutions whose failures defined the crisis (Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, AIG, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) were not commercial-bank/investment-bank hybrids created by the repeal. European universal banks, which had never been subject to Glass-Steagall-style separation, suffered parallel losses. Empirical reviews (including the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission majority report and subsequent academic assessments) treat the repeal as, at most, a background factor that modestly enlarged some conglomerates, not as a causal driver.

CONFIDENCE: 78

No. Natural resource wealth does not inherently curse economic growth. Early cross-country work (notably Sachs and Warner) found slower growth in resource-intensive economies in the 1970–1990 period, but that result is not robust.

Later research shows the association depends heavily on measurement and context. Resource *dependence* (exports as a share of GDP) is often negatively correlated with growth, but that measure is partly endogenous to poor performance in other sectors. Resource *abundance* (stocks or rents per capita), once institutions and endogeneity are accounted for, is frequently unrelated to growth or positively related to it. The negative link appears mainly where institutions are already weak (rent-seeking, weak property rights, poor fiscal rules); where institutions are strong, resources are compatible with sustained growth (Norway, Botswana, Chile, Australia, Canada). Commodity-price volatility, Dutch-disease effects, and conflict risks are real channels, but they are policy- and institution-contingent rather than automatic.

Meta-analyses that correct for publication bias find the average effect near zero. High-income resource economies and several well-managed developing exporters demonstrate that resource wealth can raise income levels and need not reduce long-run growth rates. The practical implication is managerial, not fatalistic: outcomes track governance, savings of resource rents, and diversification policy more than geology.

CONFIDENCE: 78

The “China shock” research (chiefly Autor, Dorn, and Hanson) found that the surge in Chinese imports after the early 1990s caused large, geographically concentrated, and long-lasting harm to U.S. manufacturing workers and their local labor markets. Commuting zones more exposed to Chinese import competition saw bigger drops in manufacturing employment that were not offset by job gains in other local industries; affected workers experienced persistently higher unemployment, lower earnings, and reduced labor-force participation, while communities relied more on disability and other transfer payments. Adjustment was far slower and more costly than standard trade models had predicted, even though consumers overall benefited from lower prices.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Certificate-of-need laws reduce supply (fewer hospitals, beds, imaging providers and surgery centres), raise rather than lower costs/prices, and do not improve quality (often linked to unchanged or worse outcomes).

CONFIDENCE: 82

A large share of minimum-wage cost increases is typically passed through to consumer prices, with the rest mostly absorbed by lower profits rather than by large job losses.

Studies of restaurants, retail, and similar low-wage sectors commonly find pass-through on the order of one-half to three-quarters or more of the direct wage-bill increase (a well-known large-increase study for Hungary puts the split at roughly 75% consumers / 25% owners). Short-run restaurant estimates are often toward the high end of that range; some other sectors and longer horizons show less. Because measured employment and hours effects are frequently small, displaced workers do not bear most of the incidence. The bill is therefore paid mainly by buyers of minimum-wage-intensive goods and services and by firm owners. Low-wage households often still gain on net: their earnings increases usually exceed the modest extra amount they spend because of higher prices.

Estimates vary by industry, market structure, and time horizon, so there is no single universal pass-through rate.

CONFIDENCE: 68

Only a small minority of the decline. US occupational fatality rates fell by roughly four-fifths after 1970 (from about 18 deaths per 100,000 workers to roughly 3.5), continuing a multi-decade pre-OSHA downward trend. Careful empirical work (inspections, standards, and industry-level studies) finds that OSHA’s direct effects are modest—typically low-single-digit percentage reductions in injury rates, concentrated in inspected workplaces and fading over time. Because only a small share of establishments are inspected in any year and many early standards were pre-existing consensus rules, these effects explain well under one-fifth (and plausibly far less) of the aggregate drop in deaths. Larger contributions come from the shift out of high-hazard sectors, safer technology, workers’-compensation and liability incentives, rising real incomes, and improved trauma care that converts what would once have been fatalities into survivable injuries. No sharp break in the fatality trend appears at OSHA’s creation.

CONFIDENCE: 62

On net, FDA pre-market approval has made Americans worse off. The 1938 safety requirements and especially the 1962 efficacy mandate cut the flow of new drugs roughly in half and added years of delay. Economic studies (Peltzman 1973 and later work in the same tradition) find that the resulting losses—forgone treatments, higher development costs, and patients who die while waiting—exceed the gains from blocking ineffective or dangerous compounds. Visible successes such as keeping thalidomide off the U.S. market are real but smaller than the invisible mortality from drug lag and reduced innovation. Later accelerations (user fees, priority review, breakthrough designations) have narrowed but not closed the gap. Post-market learning, liability, and physician/patient choice can police quality at lower cost to progress.

CONFIDENCE: 62

Taxi medallion systems capped the number of legal cabs in a city and required an expensive, transferable license to operate one. That artificial scarcity turned medallions into high-priced assets (often financed with large loans) whose value came from restricted competition and the fares it supported.

When Uber, Lyft, and similar services entered at scale, they added large numbers of vehicles outside the medallion cap. Ride supply rose, fares and wait times fell for riders, and the scarcity rent that had propped up medallion prices disappeared. Medallion values collapsed (in New York, from peaks near $1 million to a fraction of that), and many owners who had borrowed against peak prices faced foreclosure, bankruptcy, and severe financial distress.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Occupational licensing raises the wages of workers who hold licenses (typically by roughly 10–15 percent after standard controls) by restricting entry and competition. At the same time, state-by-state differences in requirements and limited reciprocity reduce licensed workers’ interstate mobility.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Randomised evaluations (notably the set of RCTs summarised by Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman and related follow-ups) find that microcredit produces only modest increases in borrowing and small-business activity. On average it does not meaningfully raise household income or consumption, nor does it produce substantial reductions in poverty; effects are heterogeneous and concentrated among a minority of borrowers who already had stronger entrepreneurial prospects.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Decades of US criminal prohibition and heavy enforcement have not substantially reduced illicit drug use. Consumption has remained common, supply-side pressure has not produced lasting scarcity (real prices of cocaine and heroin fell for long periods while purity often rose), and major harms such as the opioid overdose crisis occurred under prohibition. Demand, social conditions, and markets matter more than arrest and incarceration volume.

Portugal’s 2001 decriminalization of personal possession (administrative sanctions plus expanded treatment and harm reduction, not commercial legalization) did not produce a surge in drug use. Use stayed near or below many European averages; HIV infections among people who inject drugs and drug-related deaths fell sharply in the following years, and more people entered treatment. Later pressures (austerity, new synthetics) show the result is not automatic or permanent, but the record does not support the claim that criminalizing users is required to keep use in check.

CONFIDENCE: 78

No. Prohibition reduced drinking and some alcohol-related harms for a time, but it did not achieve its goals and was repealed as a failure.

The 18th Amendment and Volstead Act aimed to end the manufacture, sale, and transport of alcohol in order to cut consumption, improve health and morals, and reduce crime and poverty. Measured consumption and heavy drinking did fall: cirrhosis death rates dropped sharply in the 1920s, arrests for drunkenness declined, and contemporary estimates put per-capita alcohol use well below pre-1920 levels (often cited in the range of a 30–50% drop, though illegal supply makes the figures uncertain). Those gains were incomplete and eroded. Speakeasies, home brewing, and bootlegging supplied a large black market; consumption was rising again by the late 1920s; and repeal did not produce an immediate return to the highest pre-Prohibition drinking rates, which shows both a real but limited effect and that the ban never came close to a dry society.

The costs were large and visible. Organized crime expanded around illegal alcohol, violence and corruption increased in many cities, enforcement was expensive and widely evaded, and tainted liquor caused poisonings. Tax revenue disappeared just as the Depression hit. Public and elite support collapsed; the 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition in 1933 after only 13 years. By the standard that matters for whether a policy “worked”—durable achievement of its stated aims at acceptable cost—it did not.

CONFIDENCE: 82

The empirical literature in urban economics finds that binding land-use rules of this type reduce the elasticity of housing supply and raise prices and rents, especially in high-demand metros.

Zoning, height caps, and large minimum lot sizes directly limit how many units can be built on a given parcel and where denser housing can go. Discretionary review (design review, conditional use, lengthy hearings) adds delay, uncertainty, and cost, which further discourages projects even when the zoning envelope would allow them. Cross-city indices of regulatory stringency (for example the Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index) are strongly associated with higher house prices relative to construction costs and with lower supply responses to demand shocks. Studies that compare prices to marginal construction costs (Glaeser, Gyourko, and coauthors) find large “regulatory tax” wedges in tightly zoned coastal markets and much smaller wedges where land-use rules are looser. Natural experiments and reforms—minimum-lot-size reductions, height or density upzonings, and streamlining of permitting—generally increase housing starts or units permitted; price effects are more modest and slower where demand is not constrained or where only small areas are liberalized, but the supply channel itself is consistently signed.

Amenities and local preferences can justify some rules, and regulation is partly endogenous to high prices, so magnitudes vary and not every ordinance is equally binding. The central, repeated finding is nonetheless that the regulations named in the question constrain quantity and elevate the price of housing.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Americans had fewer, older UV filters because the FDA regulates sunscreens as OTC drugs, so new filters need a costly, drug-style safety and efficacy package before they can be marketed. For years that package was not completed for modern filters already used abroad, and FDA review (even after the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act) still found the data insufficient to add them to the U.S. monograph. The EU treats sunscreens mainly as cosmetics and Australia’s regulator has long accepted many of the same newer filters, so those markets approved ingredients such as bemotrizinol and bisoctrizole much earlier.
